content: 1. Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by bacteria that spread through the air and can infect anyone. 2. In some cases, individuals may become infected with TB bacteria but do not immediately develop symptoms of the disease. 3. When the TB bacteria remain inactive in the body, the individual is considered to have a TB infection, also known as latent TB infection (LTBI). 4. People with latent TB infection do not exhibit any signs or symptoms of active TB disease and are not contagious. 5. However, individuals with latent TB infection are at risk of developing active TB disease if their immune system becomes weakened. 6. It is estimated that approximately one in four people globally have latent TB infection, most of whom remain asymptomatic and well. 7. A proportion of those with latent TB infection will progress to active TB disease, particularly if they have risk factors such as HIV infection, diabetes, or other conditions that compromise the immune system. 8. Diagnostic tests such as the tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) can identify individuals with latent TB infection. 9. Preventive treatment for TB is recommended for individuals with latent TB infection who are at high risk of developing active TB disease. 10. Several preventive treatment regimens are available, including isoniazid, rifapentine, or a combination of these drugs, administered over varying durations. 11. Completing the full course of TB preventive treatment is essential to ensure its effectiveness in reducing the risk of progression to active TB disease. 12. TB preventive treatment is a critical intervention to stop latent TB infection from progressing to active disease, thereby reducing TB transmission and improving public health outcomes.
